meta.title: Mightling — fast AI coding on your desk
meta.description: A coding agent that resolved 68 of 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks offline on one NVIDIA DGX Spark (about 69% estimated on the full set), at about 47 tokens a second. No cloud, no account, no API bill, no telemetry.

install.p02: 68 of 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks, resolved offline on one DGX Spark, at about 47 tokens a second. A coding agent, a chat assistant and a desktop app, running entirely on your own GB10. No cloud. No account. No API bill. No telemetry. How it was measured

new.h201: New in 1.7: the desktop app on a Mac, Linux and Windows
new.p02: Mightling 1.7.0's desktop app holds Ask and Work in one window. Work is a full workbench for agent sessions: a composer with files, skills and commands, a review pane to stage, revert and commit, worktrees, terminal tabs, and a file tree and file tabs beside the thread. On your other computers it is a client of your GB10, which it finds on the local network.
new.p04: From 1.7.2, the install command puts Mightling in Applications beside ling, and it opens like any other app. Apple silicon and Intel, macOS 12 or later. ling update updates it.
new.p06: On the GB10, mightling_1.7.0_arm64.deb installs the app, its launcher entry and the ling-app command, with the sandbox profile it needs:
new.p07: Then open it from the application menu, or with ling app. More.
new.p09: From 1.7.2, the PowerShell line installs the app as well, for you alone and without administrator rights, with a Start menu entry; Settings → Apps removes it; ling update updates it. Smart App Control must be off.
new.p11: The release page also carries the Mac dmg (Mightling-<version>-arm64-preview.dmg, or x64 for Intel) and the Windows installer (Mightling-Setup-<version>-x64.exe, or arm64). They are unsigned previews: downloaded in a browser, they are stopped the first time. Check each against the release's signed SHA256SUMS first.
new.li12: macOS 15 and later: drag Mightling to Applications and open it once, then System Settings › Privacy & Security › Open Anyway. On macOS 14 and earlier, Control-click the app › Open.
new.li13: Windows: SmartScreen › More info › Run anyway. Smart App Control must be off.
new.p14: Also in 1.7.0: Night Shift can try a task several times and keep the best attempt (/night add --best-of N), one machine can run several Signal bridges, and a client chooses between two nodes on one network without losing the one it knows. Release notes and downloads.
benchmark.h201: SWE-bench Verified, measured on one DGX Spark
benchmark.p02: On 2026-10-08, Mightling 1.5.1's agent with Qwen3.8-27B resolved 68 of 100 SWE-bench Verified tasks on one DGX Spark, offline: a fixed sample of 100 tasks, one attempt per task, default mode. Scaled to all 500 tasks, that is an estimated ≈69% (95% band 63.9–73.4%). This is our own measurement, on our own machine and on a subset, not a leaderboard entry.

benchmark.p29: Read it as company, not a ranking. On the same 100 tasks Mightling resolved as many as Qwen3-Coder-480B and GLM-4.6, models many times its size, but every row uses a different agent, different hardware and, for the leaderboard rows, the official x86 test images, where ours ran on community arm64 images. In refine mode a first session studies the task without changing anything and a fresh session does it: it resolved one task more than the default (69 against 68, each arm winning tasks the other lost), at about 2.2 times the time per task, so it stays opt-in (ling --refine).
benchmark.p31: 100 tasks are a fifth of Verified, so the full-set figure is an estimate. A one-parameter item-response (Rasch) model is fitted on the per-task results of all 175 public Verified submissions: every task gets a difficulty and every system an ability. Mightling's ability is the one that explains 68 resolved on these 100 tasks; ≈69% is that ability's expected score on all 500 (a plain regression on the published scores agrees to within a point). To check it, every public submission was scored on these 100 tasks alone and its overall score predicted the same way: the error was 2.4 points (RMSE), and the band above is ±1.96 times that. Every number in the table is reproduced by scripts/swe_bench_compare.py from the public per-task data of SWE-bench/experiments.
benchmark.p32: The 100 tasks are spread across Verified's repositories in proportion to the full set, among the tasks whose test environment runs and validates on arm64 (the gold patch passes, an empty change fails). Published systems score 1.0 to 1.5 points lower on these 100 than on all 500, so the sample is not an easy one. It is not a leaderboard entry: those are graded by the SWE-bench team on their own infrastructure.

try.p02: Or queue work for tonight with /night add <task>: Mightling works through the queue while you sleep, each task on its own git branch, and you review the branches over coffee.
proof.h201: Your code never leaves your desk — and you can prove it
proof.p02: Cloud coding agents send your source code to someone else's servers. Mightling sends it nowhere: the model runs on your GB10, and nothing in Mightling phones home. No usage analytics, no metrics, no sign-in, no "anonymous" crash reports. That makes it usable for code you're not allowed to upload: client work, regulated data, unreleased products.
proof.p03: One command runs a real Mightling session under strace and lists every network connection it made:
proof.p04: Everything stayed on 127.0.0.1. Not one DNS lookup.
proof.p06: Type /airgapped on and every command the agent runs gets an empty network namespace from the Linux kernel. It isn't a polite request to the model: there is simply no network to reach. Full Access, which would bypass the sandbox, is refused at the same time.
proof.p08: Only what you or the agent asks for: a web search (through a private SearXNG on your own machine), a page fetch, a read-only request to a Google account you connected, or an update check. At /airgapped on, none of it.
why.p03: The model, your code, your prompts and your answers stay on the machine they're on.
why.p14: Single stream on a GB10 with speculative decoding. Agent work is measured over real agent sessions; code, JSON and prose by kind of output, with greedy decoding. Run four agents at once: no quota, no "please wait".
why.li16: No tuning: model, context, kernels and speculative decoding are chosen for the GB10.
why.li17: It won't freeze your machine: the host is checked and memory pressure watched during the load.
why.li18: Your other machines find it on the local network.
features.p03: Reads your repository, runs commands and tests, edits code, and asks before anything risky.
features.p05: /night add <task> before bed; each task done on its own git branch by morning. Nothing is merged or pushed without you.
features.p07: Through a private SearXNG on your own machine: no search account, no API key.
features.p09: Definitions, callers and impact across your repository, so the agent finds code instead of grepping for it.
features.p11: Skills you already wrote for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw or Hermes work unchanged.
features.p13: Questions with web search, image search and dictation, and your agent sessions, from this machine or a paired phone, on the same local model.
features.p15: Ask and Work in one window, on the GB10, a Mac, Linux or Windows: agent sessions with approvals, a review pane, worktrees and undo. New in 1.7.
features.p17: Read-only, through a sign-in that stays on your machine. Switched off entirely at /airgapped on.
machines.p02: They share the chip, the 128 GB of unified memory and DGX OS 7, so one installer covers them all. Mightling is developed and tested daily on the ASUS Ascent GX10; the others are covered by tests.
paper.h302: Architecting Local, Air-Gap-Capable Desktop Clients for Agentic AI Pair Programmers: Protocol Compatibility, Process Isolation, and Host Memory Safety
paper.p04: We present the architectural design, formal capability model, and empirical evaluation of Mightling Desktop, an open-source desktop environment that speaks the same app-server protocol as the upstream vendor's desktop client, keeps Codex-compatible defaults, runs inference on the user's own hardware, and confines every sandboxed command to the workstation when the user turns /airgapped on.
faq.p03: Yes, to run the model. Your other computers use it as clients: Linux (Arm or x86) and macOS with the same install command, Windows (Arm or x86, preview) with the PowerShell line.
faq.summary04: I installed Puffin. Is this it?
faq.p05: Yes: Puffin was renamed Mightling in 1.5. Run puffin update once, then puffin one last time. It moves your sessions, settings and links over, and from then on the command is ling.
faq.p07: Yes. Mightling is open source under the AGPL, and the model's weights are free. Your only running cost is the electricity.
faq.summary08: What do I need besides the machine?
faq.p09: The OS it ships with (DGX OS 7, or Ubuntu 24.04 where the vendor offers it), Docker with the NVIDIA Container Toolkit, Python 3 and Git. On plain Ubuntu, ling-admin host check tells you what's missing.
faq.summary10: Does anything ever reach the internet?
faq.p11: Only what you or the agent asks for, such as a web search through SearXNG on your own machine, and the first-time downloads. /airgapped on turns all of it off.
faq.p13: Qwen3.8-27B in NVIDIA's 4-bit NVFP4 format, served by SGLang with a DFlash2 drafter, chosen and tuned for the GB10. About 20 GB of weights; roughly 38 GB of the machine's memory stays free while it serves.
cta.h201: Keep your code on your desk
cta.p02: If you believe code should stay on the desk it was written on, star the repository: it's how other GB10 owners find Mightling.
